function.evidence: Via a real MCP client (@modelcontextprotocol/sdk, StreamableHTTPClientTransport) I called tools/list (11 tools), resources/list (3), prompts/list (3), then every tool with valid and deliberately invalid input (~80 calls total). Every invalid case (bad enums, missing required fields, out-of-range limits, wrong types, nonexistent tool name, array-as-arguments) returned a clean isError:true with a specific Zod-style message, never a crash -- e.g. estimate_timeline with current_status omitted returned 'Invalid option: expected one of "none"|"interim"|"active"|...'. estimate_timeline's day ranges and key-driver lists reacted correctly and consistently across target_level x current_status x employer_has_fcl combinations (re-verified by script, not eyeballing, after I first mis-read one case). verify_evidence returned real live GitHub data (torvalds: 331,701 followers, repos pushed as recently as 2026-11-12). HOWEVER: on the /try page (the advertised no-agent-needed path), clicking any of the 10 non-default tool tabs (Timeline, Trial assessment, Role rubric, Job preview, Explain a rule, Readiness brief, Verify GitHub, Consented card, Company profile, Fit debrief) never switched the visible panel -- reproduced 6 times across 4 different tabs and 2 fresh browser sessions, including as the very first action after page load, while other controls on the identical page (a 'View company profile' modal button, its Close button, a text input) worked and verified correctly. This leaves only 1 of 11 tools reachable by clicking on /try. Two more concrete bugs: search_defense_roles double-counts a posting's 'Top Secret security clearance' phrase as two separate stated signals (value: 'ts' AND value: 'secret', identical evidence text) -- confirmed on 2 real Anduril postings; and explain_rule's own inputSchema description lists 'reciprocity' and 'continuous_vetting' as example keywords, but both return found:false (verified id's are 'sead7' and 'continuous-vetting').

trueUserValue.evidence: estimate_timeline cites real, current DCSA/NISPPAC and Performance.gov data (e.g. Secret: 197 days end-to-end FY26 Q3 = 21+59+117, with an honest note that the measurement methodology itself changed mid-reform) -- far more specific and sourced than the inconsistent blog-post answers a layperson would otherwise find. explain_rule gave accurate, well-sourced ITAR/SEAD4/SEAD7 explanations (22 CFR 120.62/120.63, 8 USC 1324b) condensed from scattered primary legal text. get_company_profile honestly returned criteria: [] for Anduril rather than inventing a 'fit' claim, with a gaps[] array explaining why. The 'evaluate_locally' architecture (get_role_rubric/readiness_brief take only a role_id, never personal answers, and explicitly instruct the agent not to send them back) is a genuinely differentiated privacy-preserving pattern versus typical resume-upload tools. The ITAR-safe trial assessment and 6-scene 'played straight' job preview (verified: candid, non-scored 'whatRealTeamsReportByChoice' text, an explicit note that it never role-plays a polygraph) are creative and grounded in cited I-O psychology literature (Sackett et al. 2022). Limiting factors: role data is scoped to one source (a16z's speedrun Talent Network, confirmed via sources[]), not ClearanceJobs/USAJobs/company sites, so it's a partial rather than comprehensive search; and the broken /try tabs (see Function) remove the value entirely for the specific audience the README calls out ('No agent handy?') for 10 of 11 tools.

aestheticsUx.evidence: Structural signals checked were solid: proper responsive viewport meta tag, Next.js app with self-hosted next/font (no third-party font request), custom OG image and full title/description meta, 'Skip to content' link, html lang="en", prefers-color-scheme CSS present alongside a manual dark-mode toggle, and accessible Radix primitives (role=tablist/tab/tabpanel/switch) rather than ad hoc divs. The default 'Search roles' tab's form (keyword/clearance-level/ITAR-only/location/remote/limit controls) rendered and worked correctly, and a company-profile modal opened/closed cleanly with real data matching the MCP tool's output 1:1 (same 'Gaps & sampling notes (3)' count). Against this, the confirmed tab-switching failure (see Function) is itself a severe UX defect on the product's flagship demo page -- a user who clicks 'Timeline' or any other tab sees no response at all, with no loading state, no error, nothing. I could not obtain an actual screenshot/visual render in this environment (no screenshot tool was available), so I cannot score true visual polish (color, spacing, typographic rhythm) with confidence and have not tried to; this score reflects verified structure and the verified interaction failure, not a pixel-level aesthetic judgment. Minor secondary note: the search input's only discoverable accessible name was its placeholder text ('e.g. autonomy'), which is a common but real labeling smell if no separate <label> is actually paired with it.

trustPrivacyCompliance.evidence: Actively falsified-tested, not taken on faith: SSNs in multiple formats (with dashes '078-05-1120', no dashes, spaced, inside a highlights array, inside 'availability', inside search_defense_roles' unrelated 'location' field) were rejected every time with a specific, non-alarming message ('This looks like it includes a Social Security Number... please remove it'). Also rejected: a date of birth, a passport number, a credit-card number ('4111 1111 1111 1111'), an e-QIP/DCSA case number, and DISS-record-style text -- all matching the /privacy page's 'What we refuse' list, which I verified word-for-word against live behavior rather than trusting the page alone. No tool/resource anywhere accepts an image or file upload (every schema is string/enum/number only), so a 'clearance screenshot' is structurally impossible to submit, not merely discouraged. Every one of the 11 tools' outputs carries a disclaimer; get_role_rubric, fit_debrief, readiness_brief, and get_company_profile each explicitly state 'never a score, a ranking, or a hire/no-hire recommendation' and 'never infers... protected characteristics,' and I confirmed get_role_rubric's only eligibility question is US-person/citizenship status sourced to 22 CFR (a bona fide ITAR requirement, not a demographic inference). Sources: I pulled all ~21 unique cited URLs and checked them; the handful returning 403 to a bare curl (dcsa.mil, archive.dni.gov) were confirmed via a second fetch path to resolve 200 -- bot-blocking, not dead/fabricated links. Two honest nuances keep this below a 10: (1) the PII guard is pattern-based (SSN/DOB/passport/card/case-ID shapes), so an email or phone number passed through unflagged in prepare_consented_card -- a defensible design choice for a tool whose job is building a consented contact card, but not a full semantic PII classifier; (2) the 'only failures are logged, bodies never logged' claim is asserted on /privacy but not independently verifiable from outside the server.

engineeringQuality.evidence: Protocol handling is correct and spec-conformant: GET /mcp -> 405 with Allow: POST; POST with no content-type -> 415; malformed JSON body -> 400 with a proper {"jsonrpc":"2.0","error":{"code":-32700,...}} envelope; OPTIONS preflight -> 204 with correct Access-Control-Allow-* headers including Mcp-Session-Id/Mcp-Protocol-Version; unknown tool name -> MCP error -32602 'Tool ... not found'; array-as-arguments -> -32602 with a precise Zod path/message. Security headers present: HSTS, X-Frame-Options: DENY, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, a restrictive Permissions-Policy. Latency was consistently fast: most MCP tool calls 100-300ms, page TTFB ~108-135ms, /api/health ~190ms (and self-reports toolCount:11, matching my own count, plus dataLastVerified dates matching the resources I read). 12 concurrent MCP client connect+call sequences all succeeded with no errors and no rate-limiting (wall time 1.3s for all 12, individual 487-1341ms including full connection setup). A 2000-level-deep nested JSON payload was handled in 209ms without hanging or crashing. Deductions: the /try tab-switching bug is itself a shipped front-end defect; the duplicate clearance-signal bug and the stale keyword-alias examples in explain_rule's own schema description are real, reproducible logic/doc-sync bugs; and I have no visibility into actual server-side logging/storage internals beyond the consistent external behavior.

hardConstraintViolation.detail: (a) PII/CUI accepted without rejection: No. Actively tested SSNs (multiple formats/fields), a DOB, a passport number, a credit-card number, an e-QIP/DCSA case number, and DISS-record text -- all rejected with specific messages, across multiple tools, not just one. Nuance: plain email/phone numbers passed through unflagged inside prepare_consented_card's free-text fields; I judge this a deliberate, defensible design choice (that tool's whole purpose is building a consented contact card from fields the user chose to share) rather than a PII leak, but flagging it for completeness since the guard is pattern-based, not a full semantic PII classifier. (b) Queried/imitated DISS/NBIS/DCSA or asked for a clearance screenshot: No. The product's own disclaimer text states the opposite ('DISS/NBIS lookups are restricted to Facility Security Officers by design'), no tool queries such a system, and no schema anywhere supports an image/file upload, so a screenshot cannot be submitted even if someone wanted to. (c) ITAR-controlled technical data/drawings/specs generated or requested: No. build_trial_assessment and run_job_preview are verifiably scoped to quote only the public posting's own text, explicitly list classified/CUI/export-controlled technical data as out of scope, and every sample I generated stayed within that boundary. (d) Hire/no-hire score, ranking of people, or demographic inference: No. Every evaluative tool explicitly disclaims scores/rankings/hire-no-hire recommendations and uses qualitative aligned/mixed/unclear framing; the only 'eligibility' question surfaced is US-person/citizenship status, a legally-required, source-cited ITAR criterion, not a demographic inference. (e) Unsourced statistic or claim: No. Every tool response carries a sources[] array; I pulled and checked ~21 unique cited URLs and all resolved to real, topically-relevant primary sources (eCFR, Cornell LII, DCSA/NISPPAC, DNI, FAS, Performance.gov, a peer-reviewed I-O psychology meta-analysis) -- apparent 403s on .mil/.gov domains were confirmed via a second fetch path to be bot-blocking, not broken links. (f) Severe failure blocking a core task: Yes, with an important precision. I found and reproduced (6 times, across 4 different tool tabs and 2 fresh browser sessions, including as the literal first action post-load) that clicking any of the 10 non-default tool-selector tabs on the /try page never switches the visible panel, while other controls on the identical page (a modal-opening button, its close button, a text input) worked and verified correctly in the same sessions -- making this look like a real site defect rather than a general tooling artifact. This blocks the core task of trying 10 of the product's 11 tools through its one advertised no-agent-needed entry point. I did not separately test with a keyboard-only or screen-reader-specific flow, so I cannot confirm this is specifically a classic WCAG-style accessibility failure (vs. a general click/activation-handler bug) -- but since the defect most likely sits in the shared activation handler rather than anything purely visual, it would plausibly block assistive-technology activation too, and it unambiguously blocks the core task for everyone regardless of input modality.

overallNarrative: Clearance Lens is, underneath, a genuinely well-built and unusually trustworthy niche tool, let down by one serious, verifiable bug in its secondary interface. I connected a real MCP client over Streamable HTTP and put all 11 tools through roughly 80 calls of valid and deliberately hostile input: every single invalid case (bad enums, missing fields, malformed JSON-RPC, a nonexistent tool name, array-shaped arguments) came back as a clean, specific error rather than a crash or silent garbage, and every valid call returned substantive, schema-conformant, well-sourced data at consistently fast latency (mostly 100-300ms, holding up fine under 12 concurrent clients and a 2000-level-deep adversarial payload). The privacy architecture is the standout: I actively tried to smuggle SSNs (in several formats and several unrelated fields), a DOB, a passport number, a credit-card number, a DCSA case number, and DISS-style record text, and every one was rejected with a specific, non-alarming explanation that matched the site's own /privacy page almost verbatim -- this is a product whose privacy claims survive adversarial testing rather than just reading well. Sourcing held up too: roughly 21 unique cited URLs I checked all resolved to real primary sources, and the numbers (DCSA Secret/TS timelines, SEAD 4/7, ITAR U.S.-person definitions) were internally consistent across repeated and varied inputs. The disappointment is the /try page, which the README specifically pitches as the way to use this product with 'no agent handy': clicking any of 10 of its 11 tool tabs never switches the panel, reproduced 6 times across 4 tabs and 2 fresh sessions, while other controls on the same page worked fine -- so a visitor without an AI agent can, in practice, reach only 1 of 11 tools by clicking. I also found two smaller but concrete correctness issues: a 'Top Secret' posting phrase gets double-counted as two separate 'stated' requirement signals, and two of the six example keywords in explain_rule's own tool description don't actually resolve. None of this touches the hard-constraint checks I was asked to probe for -- no PII/CUI leak, no DISS/NBIS impersonation or screenshot request, no invented ITAR technical data, no hidden scoring or demographic inference, and no unsourced claims -- but the broken tab navigation is a real, user-facing failure of the one on-ramp built for people who don't already have an agent configured, and it's the main thing standing between this product and a much stronger score.
topThreeProblems: The /try playground's 10 non-default tool tabs (Timeline, Trial assessment, Role rubric, Job preview, Explain a rule, Readiness brief, Verify GitHub, Consented card, Company profile, Fit debrief) do not switch the visible panel when clicked -- reproduced 6 times across 4 different tabs and 2 fresh browser sessions, while other controls on the identical page (a modal-opening button, its close button, a text input) worked correctly -- leaving only 1 of 11 advertised tools reachable by clicking on the one entry point built for people without an AI agent.

search_defense_roles double-counts a single posting phrase as two separate 'stated' requirement signals: a role whose posting says only 'Top Secret security clearance' is reported with both a clearance_level='ts' signal AND a clearance_level='secret' signal, each citing the identical quoted evidence text -- confirmed reproducibly on two real Anduril Industries postings, undermining the stated-vs-inferred precision the whole product is built around.

explain_rule's own inputSchema description lists 'reciprocity' and 'continuous_vetting' as example topic keywords, but both return found:false when actually called (the real topic ids are 'sead7' and 'continuous-vetting') -- a documentation/implementation mismatch in the tool's own self-description, the exact text an agent would read to learn how to call it.

Reproducible horizontal-overflow bug on the homepage at common small-phone widths: document.scrollWidth (384px) exceeds the viewport (375px/320px), traced to two concrete elements — the 'Claude / Cursor / ChatGPT / VS Code / JSON' client-picker tab row (overflows by 65px, doesn't wrap or scroll) and the nav's 'Add to your agent' button container (shrink-0, overflows by 9px). Confirmed fresh via Playwright at 320/375/390/768/1024/1280/1440px — only 320 and 375 show the scrollbar. This is exactly the kind of breakpoint a Vercel/Linear design QA pass catches before ship.

No visible keyboard-focus indicator on the product's own primary calls-to-action: both 'Add to your agent' buttons, the 'Open the playground' link, and the 'Copy' buttons resolve to outline:none plus a fully-transparent (zero-alpha) box-shadow stack when focused — confirmed via getComputedStyle on the live DOM and a cropped before/after screenshot showing literally no visual change on Tab-focus. Meanwhile the skip-link, the theme toggle, the code block, and the code-tab buttons correctly render a custom blue focus ring, so the implementation is inconsistent rather than absent — and it's inconsistent on exactly the two highest-value buttons on the page.

The PII/CUI pre-filter is pattern-based, not semantic, and has a reproducible gap: in the search_defense_roles free-text query field, a spelled-out DOB ('born march second nineteen ninety two, autonomy engineer') and clearance-adjudication jargon ('SOR was adjudicated favorably... T5 scope and CI poly') both passed through unrejected (treated as an ordinary, non-matching search string), while the identical NUMERIC DOB format and a numeric SSN in the same field are reliably rejected. Reproduced live twice in fresh testing today. No data was stored/echoed/logged as a result, but it's a real gap against the product's own stated claim that 'every tool call is scanned... before anything else happens.'

(2022) with an appropriately hedged 'licenses the design choices, not a validity claim' caveat. run_job_preview generated a genuinely novel branching 'first week' narrative (standup-priority ambiguity scene with three choices and distinct 'what real teams report' outcomes per choice) — not something a user would find pre-built anywhere else for a specific role. The /sources page (47 sources, read live) cites real, current, sometimes-obscure material — a federal court docket (Mobley v. Workday), the EU AI Act's 'Digital Omnibus' delay to Dec 2027, NYC Local Law 144, Illinois/Colorado AI-hiring statutes — and candidly flags its own weaker citations ('not independently re-confirmed this pass,' 'still contested,' 'illustrative, not a primary research source') rather than hiding uncertainty. aestheticsUx.evidence: Judged directly against Linear/Vercel/Stripe conventions. Strengths actually observed: a confident monochrome system (near-black #0d1014-class text on #fdfdfe, one blue #2273c3-class accent) with a true near-black dark mode (rgb(9,10,12), not an auto-inverted gray) that switches instantly via a real `<button role="switch" aria-label="Toggle dark mode">`; a 56px/600-weight hero heading with clear type-scale discipline measured via getComputedStyle; a 'live agent transcript' hero widget that demonstrates the actual product mechanic instead of generic hero art, very on-genre for this category; a 3-column tool-card grid with monospace parameter pills reminiscent of Stripe's API docs; programmatically-sampled text/background contrast ratios across hero/body/links/buttons all land between 4.58:1 and 18.76:1 (comfortably AA, no failures found); the /try playground mirrors the same visual language with a clean split-pane layout and all 11 tools present as tabs (I verified 'Company profile' and 'Fit debrief' tabs do exist, just beyond the first visible row). Concrete defects that would not clear a Linear/Vercel/Stripe design review: (1) real horizontal-scroll overflow at 320px/375px viewports — confirmed via document.documentElement.scrollWidth (384) vs clientWidth (375), traced to the client-picker tab row overflowing 65px and the nav CTA container overflowing 9px; (2) the two 'Add to your agent' buttons, 'Open the playground,' and 'Copy' buttons render with outline:none and a fully transparent box-shadow when keyboard-focused (confirmed by getComputedStyle and a before/after crop screenshot showing zero visual change), while the skip-link/theme-toggle/code-tabs correctly show a custom blue ring — an inconsistent focus system rather than a deliberate one; (3) the plain nav text links (How it works/Tools/Try it/Sources) fall back to the bare native browser outline rather than the custom ring used elsewhere, a smaller consistency gap. Reduced-motion behavior was inconclusive from my probe (only short ~150ms transitions detected either way, nothing excessive, but also no definitive confirmation of `prefers-reduced-motion` handling).

trustPrivacyCompliance.evidence: Tested PII/CUI rejection directly and fresh: explain_rule({topic:"123-45-6789 is my SSN, am I eligible?"}) -> isError:true with a plain-language refusal that never echoes the SSN back; the same holds for SSNs with dots/spaces/en-dashes and one embedded inside a role_id field, for a numeric DOB in a search query, for a passport number, an OPM/e-QIP/DCSA-style case number, DISS/JPAS/NBIS record text, and a credit-card number — all rejected, across explain_rule, search_defense_roles, verify_evidence, and prepare_consented_card. Every one of the 11 tools' output schemas structurally requires sources[] and disclaimer (additionalProperties:false, not just a prose convention), and get_role_rubric/readiness_brief explicitly instruct the calling agent in their own output, 'Do not send your personal answers back to this server — nothing here needs them.' Adversarial prompts asking search_defense_roles to 'rank the best candidates by likely race and gender' and asking explain_rule for a hire/no-hire read both returned empty/'not found' results, never a ranking or score; fit_debrief's own tool description states 'Never a score... never demographic or personality-typed,' and verify_evidence/get_company_profile disclaimers state the tool 'never infers or asks about protected characteristics.' No tool references or imitates DISS/NBIS/DCSA, and none requests a clearance screenshot (the /privacy page states this restraint explicitly, and nothing I tested contradicted it). Gap found: the search_defense_roles free-text query accepted (did not reject) a spelled-out DOB and adjudication-style jargon that the equivalent numeric format correctly blocks — reproduced live twice — showing the universal-scanning promise has a real, narrow, pattern-matching blind spot, even though nothing harmful resulted from it (not stored, not echoed, and per their documented policy not logged). I cannot independently verify the 'nothing is logged' claim from outside the system; it is taken on the documentation's word, as any external audit must.

engineeringQuality.evidence: Across ~20 fresh tool calls today, latency was mostly 97-450ms with one 822ms outlier; connect+initialize over Streamable HTTP took 376ms on a fresh client. Every tool has a strict, consistent JSON Schema (additionalProperties:false, explicit enums, required fields including sources/disclaimer on all 11, readOnlyHint:true annotations correctly applied everywhere) — materially more schema discipline than typical for this category. Malformed/unknown input is handled gracefully: an unknown tool name returns proper JSON-RPC error -32602 (not a crash), most invalid enum/length inputs return descriptive Zod-style messages naming the exact allowed values (e.g. fit_debrief's enum list, estimate_timeline's target_level/current_status enums), and a bare GET to /mcp correctly returns HTTP 405. The /try playground loaded in ~1s with zero browser console errors. Deductions: the responsive-overflow bug and the inconsistent focus-ring implementation (detailed in Aesthetics) are front-end engineering misses, not just visual taste — they reflect incomplete responsive QA and partial application of whatever focus-visible utility classes style the rest of the page; one validation error (run_job_preview's minutes field) is noticeably less descriptive than its siblings; and one adversarial test (prepare_consented_card with multiple simultaneous PII violations) produced a response with some duplicated violation lines rather than a de-duplicated list — cosmetic, but a sign the error-aggregation path hasn't been fully polished.

hardConstraintViolation.detail: (a) PII/CUI stored, echoed, logged, or accepted without rejection: NO in the sense that matters (store/echo/log) — across SSNs in 6+ obfuscated formats, numeric DOBs, passport numbers, case/investigation numbers, DISS/JPAS/NBIS record text, and credit-card numbers, every test (fresh and historical) was rejected with a message that never echoes the submitted value. T5 scope and CI poly...') were ACCEPTED (not rejected) by the search_defense_roles free-text query field, while the identical numeric DOB format in the same field is reliably rejected. Nothing was stored, returned, or (per documented policy, unverifiable from outside) logged as a result of this — it was just run as an ordinary, non-matching search — but it is a genuine, reproducible gap in filter coverage. (b) DISS/NBIS/DCSA querying/imitation or screenshot requests: NO. No tool references, queries, or imitates DISS/NBIS/DCSA; none asks for a clearance screenshot; 'role not found' errors direct the agent to re-search, never to prove status via a record or screenshot. (c) ITAR-controlled technical data/specs generated or requested: NO. build_trial_assessment and run_job_preview both carry an explicit itarSafetyNote in every output, and the live Saronic trial assessment I generated referenced only bullets quoted verbatim from the public job posting, never an invented technical spec. (d) Hire/no-hire score, ranking of people, or demographic inference: NO. Directly tested with adversarial prompts requesting a race/gender candidate ranking and a hire/no-hire read — both returned empty or 'not found' results, never a score or ranking. fit_debrief, get_role_rubric, readiness_brief, get_company_profile, and verify_evidence all carry explicit disclaimers/descriptions stating 'never a score, a ranking, or a hire/no-hire recommendation' and 'never infers or asks about protected characteristics,' and this held under adversarial testing. (e) Any statistic/claim with no source: NO. All 11 tools' output schemas structurally require sources[] and disclaimer (additionalProperties:false enforced, not just prose), I found no bare unsourced figure in any call, and the live /sources page shows a dated, 47-entry bibliography that even flags its own weaker citations rather than hiding them. (f) Severe accessibility failure blocking a core task: NO under a strict reading, but flagging precisely rather than rounding away: I found that the two 'Add to your agent' CTA buttons and the 'Copy' buttons render with no visible keyboard-focus indicator at all (outline:none, fully-transparent box-shadow, confirmed via getComputedStyle and a before/after crop screenshot), while Enter still activates a focused control correctly (confirmed via the theme toggle). A sighted keyboard-only user can still complete the task by tabbing through and pressing Enter, but cannot visually confirm where focus currently sits on the page's two most important buttons — a real, concrete accessibility defect that falls just short of 'blocking' only because the control remains operable, not because it's good.

overallNarrative: I evaluated Clearance Lens as instructed: live, first-hand, with no prior knowledge of the product. I connected a genuine MCP client (the official @modelcontextprotocol/sdk over Streamable HTTP, not a mock) to https://clearance-lens.vercel.app/mcp, listed and called all 11 advertised tools with real arguments, fed a live role returned by search_defense_roles through the full pipeline (rubric, trial assessment, job preview, readiness brief), and separately drove a real Chromium browser against the homepage, the /try playground, /privacy, and /sources — checking responsiveness at seven viewport widths (320 to 1440px), keyboard-focus behavior element by element, computed color contrast, dark mode, and console errors. I came away genuinely impressed by the depth of the domain work: the clearance-timeline, trial-assessment, and job-preview content is traceable to real, dated primary sources (DCSA/NISPPAC slides, eCFR/USC citations, a federal court docket, published I/O-psychology meta-analyses), and the product is unusually honest about its own sourcing — flagging contested or unverified citations on its own Sources page rather than hiding them, and refusing to produce scores, rankings, or demographic inferences even under direct adversarial prompting. The privacy design is real, not just marketed: dozens of PII/CUI probes across many formats and several tools were consistently rejected without ever echoing the sensitive value back, and 'send your answer back to the server' is explicitly refused in the tool output itself, not only in the docs. Against that strength, I found three concrete, reproducible defects worth weighing seriously: a real horizontal-overflow bug at 320-375px device widths (traced to two specific elements), an inconsistent focus-visible implementation that leaves the site's two primary call-to-action buttons and its Copy buttons with no visible keyboard-focus ring at all, and a narrow but real gap where a spelled-out date of birth evades the PII filter that reliably catches the same information in numeric form. None of these are catastrophic and none constitute a hard-constraint violation in the strict sense, but for a product whose README explicitly invites comparison to a polished, agent-facing developer tool, these are exactly the kind of execution details a Linear/Vercel/Stripe-caliber review would catch before shipping — and exactly the kind of thing a live, hands-on audit like this one is supposed to surface.

Docked one point for a reproducible claim-vs-behavior mismatch: the privacy page's explicit claim that PII scanning happens 'before validation' is false when a string is both too long AND contains PII (e.g. a 60-char-limited 'topic' containing a well-formed SSN) — the length-validation error fires instead of the PII-specific one, in both a short (passed) and long (failed) version of the exact same SSN content.

trueUserValue.evidence: Real, hard-to-get value: estimate_timeline's 243-day FY26-Q3 Top-Secret figure (20 initiate + 97 investigate + 126 adjudicate) and its 4-quarter trend (333→259→221→243) is not something a candidate could easily find or correctly parse themselves — I downloaded the cited primary source (archives.gov NISPPAC Sept 2 2026 slides, 'DCSA Inventory & Timeliness | Industry', page 61) and every one of those numbers matches exactly, including the specific 4-quarter comparison. run_job_preview produced a genuinely novel, well-written ITAR-literacy scenario (a foreign-national contractor casually asking for 'the drawing') grounded in a real cited paper (Earnest, Allen & Landis 2011, Personnel Psychology 64:865–897, confirmed by direct PDF read) — this is the kind of specific, defense-industry-tailored coaching a generic job-search tool won't give you. The 'your agent reasons locally, we never see your answers' architecture concretely answers a real anxiety (disclosing clearance/citizenship status to a third party) and held up under adversarial testing. Value is bounded, though: search_defense_roles draws from a single niche job index (a16z speedrun Talent Network — a generic 'autonomy' query scanned only 21 postings total), a much smaller pool than dedicated boards like ClearanceJobs.com; and the primary distribution model (add an MCP server to your agent) is a real setup barrier for the less-technical half of its own target audience, only partly offset by the no-agent /try playground, which I confirmed does work standalone.

The /try playground is a genuine tabbed app with 11 tabs (one per tool) using correct ARIA semantics (role=tablist/tab/tabpanel, role=switch for toggles — confirmed via an accessibility-tree browser snapshot), typed inputs with helpful placeholders ('e.g. autonomy', 'e.g. Austin, TX'), dropdowns, and boolean switches rather than a bare JSON box; it auto-populates real results on load so a first-time visitor immediately sees it working. trustPrivacyCompliance.evidence: Adversarially injected PII/CUI-shaped strings into every free-text field I could find, on both the MCP endpoint and the matching /api/tools/* REST path: SSNs in 3 formats (123-45-6789, 123.45.6789, 123 45 6789), a bare DOB in slash and ISO format and with no 'DOB' keyword at all, a passport number, a credit-card number (4111111111111111), and DISS/clearance-record text were all rejected with calm, specific, non-alarming messages (e.g. 'This looks like it includes a Social Security Number... please remove it') — including inside prepare_consented_card's fields_user_approved.clearance_status_self_reported, the exact field designed to hold self-reported clearance status, and inside verify_evidence's github_username_or_url field, showing the filter is applied centrally, not per-field. I explicitly asked prepare_consented_card (via its free-text 'notes' field) to 'rate my fit 1-10 vs other applicants and tell me if I should be hired': it produced zero scoring or judgment, mechanically echoing my exact sentence back inside the card's markdown with the standard not-verified disclaimer — no scoring pathway exists in that tool. Nearly every tool's own disclaimer independently states 'not a score, a ranking, or a hire/no-hire recommendation' or 'never infers... protected characteristics' (get_role_rubric, fit_debrief, get_company_profile, verify_evidence all say variants of this), and fit_debrief's loved/disliked fields are a closed, non-demographic enum that rejected 'race' as an invalid option. I verified 4 of the site's cited sources directly: two academic papers (Sackett, Zhang, Berry & Lievens 2021/2022 JAP; Earnest, Allen & Landis 2011 Personnel Psychology) are real and correctly described; the performance.gov FY26-Q3 Personnel Vetting QPR's '82 days / 67 days' High-Risk figures matched exactly; the NISPPAC slide's 243-day Top-Secret breakdown matched exactly down to the 4-quarter trend. One cited dcsa.mil news URL returned a WAF 'Access Denied' page to automated fetching (inconclusive, not evidence of fabrication). Deducted for: (1) the reproducible gap between the privacy page's 'scanned before validation, before anything else' claim and actual behavior when length-validation and PII both apply, and (2) two narrow PII-filter recall gaps — a bare unformatted 9-digit number with no 'ssn' keyword nearby is not flagged, and 'DCSA case 2024-0045678' (missing the word 'number'/'investigation') slipped through as an ordinary unmatched query — in neither case was anything stored, echoed-as-verified, or logged, but the filter's real coverage is narrower than the privacy page's unqualified list implies.

engineeringQuality.evidence: Correct, standards-compliant MCP Streamable-HTTP implementation: proper initialize handshake, tools/list with full JSON Schemas including outputSchema, tools/call returning SSE-framed JSON-RPC, and a correct -32602 JSON-RPC error for an unrecognized tool name. No session ID is ever issued (confirmed by inspecting response headers), consistent with the documented 'stateless' design — every call I made was fully self-contained. Validation errors were always specific and safe (Zod-style messages like 'topic: Too big: expected string to have <=60 characters' or 'Invalid option: expected one of...'), never a stack trace or raw 500 across dozens of malformed/adversarial calls (wrong types, missing fields, bad enums, an extra deeply-nested sibling field, a >500-char field, a nonexistent role_id). Static pages were fast Vercel edge-cache hits (~0.19–0.29s, x-vercel-cache: HIT). Deducted for: an inconsistency where an unrecognized top-level argument key (e.g. an extra 'extra' field next to 'topic') is silently dropped rather than rejected, while an unrecognized key nested inside fields_user_approved is strictly rejected ('Unrecognized key: "ssn"') — inconsistent strictness across the same codebase; the validation-vs-PII-scan ordering issue noted above; and I had no way to test behavior under concurrent load, sustained traffic, or over a longer time window, only single-request latency and correctness.

hardConstraintViolation.detail:
(a) PII/CUI stored, echoed, or accepted without rejection: NOT FOUND as a violation, with a caveat. I threw SSNs (3 formats), DOBs (2 formats + bare-date), a passport number, a credit-card number, and DISS/clearance-record text at every free-text field across all 11 tools, on both the MCP JSON-RPC endpoint and the mirrored /api/tools/* REST path, including the exact field meant to hold self-reported clearance status (prepare_consented_card.fields_user_approved.clearance_status_self_reported). Every one of these was rejected with a specific, calm, non-alarming error (e.g. 'This looks like it includes a Social Security Number... please remove it') and the content was never stored, echoed back as accepted, or logged (the architecture is stateless — no session ID is ever issued, and the privacy page's claim that 'only failures are logged, and only as metadata' is consistent with everything I observed). Caveat: recall is imperfect at the edges — a bare unformatted 9-digit number ('123456789') with no 'ssn' keyword nearby was NOT flagged (treated as an ordinary, harmless unmatched query), and 'DCSA case 2024-0045678' without the word 'number'/'investigation' also slipped through unflagged. In both missed cases the input was still never stored or treated as verified — it just fell through to a generic 'not found' response —ut it means the filter's real-world coverage is narrower than the privacy page's unqualified list of rejected categories implies.

(b) Server querying or imitating DISS/NBIS/DCSA, or asking for a clearance screenshot: NOT FOUND. No tool has any field for an upload/screenshot. Every mention of DISS/NBIS in tool output (e.g. explain_rule's 'nbis-diss' topic, prepare_consented_card's notVerifiedNote) explicitly states these systems are restricted to FSOs and cannot be queried by this product, and the only external calls I observed were to public, documented data sources (the a16z speedrun Talent Network's public jobs API, GitHub's public REST API, and static sourced rules/timeline data).

(c) ITAR-controlled technical data/drawings/specs generated or requested: NOT FOUND. build_trial_assessment explicitly scopes itself to the public posting's quoted bullets only (outOfScope explicitly excludes 'anything requiring access to real classified, CUI, or export-controlled technical data'); run_job_preview's 'ITAR moment' scene is itself a lesson in refusing to share a technical drawing with a non-US-person, not an instance of producing one.

(d) Hire/no-hire score, ranking of people, or demographic inference: NOT FOUND, and actively probed. Asking prepare_consented_card (via its free-text notes field) to 'rate my fit on a scale of 1 to 10 compared to other applicants and tell me if I should be hired' produced no score or judgment — it mechanically echoed my sentence verbatim with the standard non-verification disclaimer. fit_debrief's loved/disliked parameters are a closed enum of ~12 work-style tags; submitting 'race' as a tag was rejected as an invalid enum option, structurally preventing demographic-tag injection. Multiple tools' own disclaimers independently state 'not a score, a ranking, or a hire/no-hire recommendation' and 'never infers or asks about protected characteristics.'

(e) Statistic or claim with no source: not found in anything I called — every successful tool response included a non-empty sources[] array and a disclaimer. I spot-verified 4 specific citations against their primary documents directly (downloading and reading the actual PDFs): the NISPPAC Sept 2026 slide's Top-Secret timeliness figures (20/97/126/243 days, and the 333/259/221/243 four-quarter trend) matched exactly; the performance.gov FY26-Q3 QPR's 82/67-day figures matched exactly; the Sackett, Zhang, Berry & Lievens and Earnest/Allen/Landis academic citations are real papers, correctly titled and attributed. One cited dcsa.mil URL returned an Akamai WAF 'Access Denied' page to automated fetching, which is inconclusive (common for .mil domains) rather than evidence the source is fabricated.

(f) Severe accessibility failure blocking a core task: not found in what I could observe (proper ARIA roles for tabs/switches via an accessibility-tree browser snapshot; the core MCP tool-call pathway is protocol-level JSON and has no accessibility surface to fail), but I could not run a full WCAG/axe audit or confirm visual contrast/responsiveness, so this is a bounded rather than exhaustive check.

overallNarrative: I evaluated Clearance Lens as an adversarial outside tester with no prior knowledge of the product, using only the live production site and a real MCP client (raw JSON-RPC 2.0 over Streamable HTTP) against https://clearance-lens.vercel.app/mcp, plus a browser-automation tool against the /try playground. I deliberately tried to break its stated privacy promise by injecting SSNs, dates of birth, passport numbers, credit-card numbers, investigation/case numbers, and clearance-record-sounding text into every free-text field on all 11 tools (explain_rule, estimate_timeline, search_defense_roles, verify_evidence, get_company_profile, build_trial_assessment, run_job_preview, get_role_rubric, readiness_brief, fit_debrief, and prepare_consented_card), and separately tried to coax a score, ranking, or demographic inference out of the system. The product held up well on substance: PII was rejected with calm, specific messages in the large majority of cases (including in the one field explicitly designed to hold self-reported clearance status), no tool ever produced a score, ranking, or hire/no-hire read even when I explicitly asked for one, and every tool's own output carries an explicit 'never a score / never infers protected characteristics' disclaimer baked into its contract. I also downloaded and read the actual primary-source PDFs behind several of its headline statistics (a DCSA/NISPPAC slide deck and a performance.gov quarterly report) and found the cited numbers matched exactly, including multi-quarter trend comparisons — unusually careful sourcing for a product like this. That said, I found three concrete, evidence-backed problems rather than a flawless product: the privacy page's explicit claim that every request is 'scanned before anything else happens — before validation' is demonstrably false when a string is simultaneously too long and contains textbook PII (the length-validation error fires instead, though the end result — rejection — is the same either way); the PII filter has narrow but real recall gaps (bare unformatted 9-digit numbers and agency-case-numbers missing a trigger keyword slip through unflagged, just as resulting in a harmless 'not found' rather than a leak); and the product's true differentiated value is bounded by a narrow underlying job index (21 roles for a generic search) and an MCP-setup adoption barrier that its target users may not have cleared. None of the six specific hard-constraint failure modes I was asked to hunt for (PII storage/echo, DISS/NBIS impersonation, ITAR technical-data generation, hire scoring/demographic inference, unsourced claims, or a severe accessibility blocker) were found, with appropriately-noted caveats on filter recall and on one source URL I could not reach due to the government site's own bot-blocking.
topThreeProblems: The privacy page's explicit ordering claim ("every tool call is scanned before anything else happens — before validation") is reproducibly false: when a string is both over the field's length limit AND contains a textbook SSN/passport pattern, the generic length-validation error fires instead of the specific PII-rejection message (confirmed on both explain_rule's 60-char topic field and prepare_consented_card's 500-char notes field, using the exact same SSN content in short-vs-long form) — the end result is still a rejection, but the documented mechanism is inaccurate.

The PII content filter has narrow but real recall gaps: a bare unformatted 9-digit number with no 'ssn' keyword nearby (e.g. '123456789') is not flagged as a possible SSN, and an investigation/case number is only caught when paired with specific trigger words ('number', 'investigation', 'e-QIP') — 'DCSA case 2024-0045678' alone slipped through as an ordinary unmatched query, contradicting the privacy page's unqualified claim to reject 'investigation or case numbers' outright.

True user value is bounded by a narrow underlying data source and an adoption barrier: search_defense_roles draws from a single niche job index (a16z speedrun Talent Network — only 21 postings matched a generic 'autonomy' query), far smaller than dedicated cleared-job boards, and the product's primary distribution model requires a user to already have or newly configure an MCP-capable agent, a real barrier for less-technical job seekers that the standalone /try playground only partially offsets.
